title: Features: charts
summary:
This part settles every user-visible chart feature for the rewrite: the chart types and the calendar scale, axes and number formats, labels and series identity, legends, annotations, facets, exact values and missing data, reader interactions and readouts, the action row, expanded view and table, downloads, zoom, motion, accessibility, self-measurement diagnostics and how palettes reach charts. Daniel's FEA-CH-01 answer makes RichView the richest chart library: at least every chart type ggplot2, Plotly, ECharts, Highcharts and Power BI define, likely around 30, plus a map element, a flow element and much better normal and pivot tables. The cards here fix today's nine types; each added type gets the same treatment, and compiling the type list is TYP-14's open item. Each card is one decision: keep, change or drop, written as the final rule for the rewrite. Behaviour on `main` (`b4db233`) was verified in code, probe renders and a headless browser on 2026-10-21 and 2026-10-22; Daniel's latest chart calls (partly built on the PR #67 branch) appear as proposals or conflicts. Where `main` behaves differently on calendar charts, the card says so, and FEA-CH-74 lists every calendar-only behaviour with the card that decides it. Report blocks (04b), surfaces (04c), branch-only features (04d), field definitions (05) and style values (06) are out of scope; cards point there.

Key decisions:

- **One expanded view and a labelled action row** (FEA-CH-44, FEA-CH-68, FEA-CH-43, FEA-CH-47): one modal replaces the desktop toggle, the phone dialog and "Inspect chart", a phone held upright gets the chart turned a quarter, and Table, Download (PNG/SVG), CSV and Expand carry visible labels at every width.
- **Honest axes** (FEA-CH-19, FEA-CH-21, FEA-CH-22, FEA-CH-24, FEA-CH-25): years print as years without author effort, compaction starts at 10,000, no axis crosses zero unless the data do, zoom never rescales y, calendar ticks never subdivide below the data's spacing, and a four-digit year appears only where it changes.
- **Sparse labels** (FEA-CH-27, FEA-CH-28): series named alone at line ends, at most five point names by default, author highlights with priorities, and leaders only for forced highlights.
- **One look and one behaviour for every chart** (FEA-CH-15, FEA-CH-16, FEA-CH-74, FEA-CH-41): calendar charts become a scale in the one painter, each JSON-only feature is kept or dropped by name, and lines read every series at the nearest x anywhere over the plot.
- **Checks that catch what they miss today** (FEA-CH-30, FEA-CH-59, FEA-CH-60, FEA-CH-69): real font metrics instead of stretched text, a browser pass in `richview check` at the frame widths, checks for zero-crossing axes, year labels, tick density and chart-text contrast, and one table of checks per chart type.

How to answer: **accept** keeps the proposal as written; **edit** replaces it with your text; **reject** drops it from the rewrite (add a note with what you want instead); **defer** leaves it open. Part 08's cross-part contradiction cards (OPN-50 to OPN-68) decide conflicts involving this part's cards and should be answered first.

items.title: Nine chart types
items.question: Does the rewrite ship exactly the nine chart types on `main`: line, area, bar, scatter (with bubbles), pie, heatmap, histogram, boxplot and interval?
items.why: Sets the engine's size, the type list in T-CHART-ENCODING (TYP-14) and the fixtures behind every item in this part; a type cut here disappears from the docs, `richview learn` and the chart gallery.
items.proposed: RichView draws nine chart types and no others: `line`, `area`, `bar`, `scatter` (bubbles through `encoding.size`), `pie`, `heatmap`, `histogram`, `boxplot` and `interval`. The items below fix each type's behaviour. The docs, `richview learn` and the chart gallery list the same nine. A new type (map, waterfall, sankey, animated playback) enters only through a later lockdown answer, never on an agent's initiative.

options.label: Nine (current)
options.detail: All built, specified and covered by contracts; histogram, boxplot and interval are five days old and have no reader feedback yet.

options.label: Six (drop histogram, boxplot, interval)
options.detail: Smaller engine; loses the distribution and uncertainty charts analysts need.

options.label: Nine plus playback
options.detail: PR #62's animated controls; decided by T-CHART-CONTROLS (TYP-77), not here.

items.recommendation: Nine (current): together they cover comparison, trend, composition, distribution and uncertainty, and each already has a written contract.

items.title: Line charts
items.question: Keep line charts as on `main`: one path per series, breaks at missing values, monotone curves and direct series names?
items.why: Line is the most used type in the examples and the flagship; this fixes its default look, so an author gets it with no extra fields: good defaults carry quality (Daniel's INT-13 answer).
items.proposed: A `line` chart draws one 2.5 px path per series; `encoding.color` names the series field, and without it there is one series. Observations join in axis order using the curve in FEA-CH-03 and break at missing values (FEA-CH-38). Two or more series are named at their line ends (FEA-CH-27); a single series needs no key. The value axis follows FEA-CH-19. Numeric and nominal x share the general painter; x values that are all calendar strings get the calendar scale (FEA-CH-15).

items.title: Curves: monotone by default, straight and steps on request
items.question: Do lines and areas default to smooth curves that never overshoot the data (today's monotone curves), or to straight segments?
items.why: Daniel called the earlier curves "dodgy"; the default decides how every trend looks. Under INT-11 the curve is a presentation choice the author makes, not a fidelity rule: the observations stay in readouts, Table and CSV at the author's precision (FEA-CH-37) whatever the curve.
items.proposed: Lines and areas use shape-preserving monotone cubic curves by default: each segment stays between its two observations, so the curve never overshoots, the look the line-curvature request asked for. The curve is the author's choice and no curve is ruled out for fidelity: `style.curve` offers `linear` and three step forms (`step`, `step_before`, `step_after`) for held values such as prices and rates, and `style.curvature` (0 to 1) sets how strongly the monotone curve smooths. Whatever the curve, readouts, Table and CSV show the observations themselves at the author's precision (FEA-CH-37), never interpolated points. Stacked areas and dense mean/range envelopes keep straight boundaries.

options.label: Monotone default
options.detail: Smooth without overshoot; can soften a sharp turn between two observations, which readouts still show as observed.

options.label: Linear default
options.detail: Most literal; angular at low point counts, which Daniel disliked.

items.recommendation: Monotone default, as shipped for the line-curvature request; authors pick another curve where it reads better.

items.title: Area charts
items.question: Keep areas as translucent fills to zero, one per series, overlapping rather than stacked?
items.why: Overlapping fills hide lower series once there are more than two or three; this item fixes the default and FEA-CH-05 decides stacking.
items.proposed: An `area` chart draws each series as a line with a translucent fill down to zero; several series overlap in source order and are named at their ends like lines. The value axis always includes zero. Fill opacity is one style token (`area-opacity`) for every area chart, whatever its x scale. Missing values break the line and its fill at the same observations. A band between two series (Playfair's balance-of-trade shading) is not offered.

items.title: Stacked bars and areas
items.question: Does the rewrite offer stacked bars and stacked areas? On `main` no `.rmd` bar or area chart can stack; only histograms stack their colour groups.
items.why: Composition over categories or time (revenue by segment) is a common management chart; without stacking, authors fall back to overlapping areas or grouped bars that hide the total.
items.proposed: Bars and areas are unstacked by default. `stack: true` (TYP-12, D-TYP-TEMPORAL-FEATURES) stacks them: each `encoding.color` group sits on the previous one in legend order, negative values stack downwards from zero, and the stack top carries the total in readouts while each layer shows its own value. Layers and total are each rounded to the chart's precision (FEA-CH-37), so the shown layers need not add up to the shown total. Stacked areas keep straight layer boundaries. Hiding a layer restacks the rest.

options.label: No stacked bars or areas (current `.rmd`)
options.detail: Smallest; composition needs facets or a pie.

options.label: Opt-in stacking for bars and areas
options.detail: Covers composition; middle layers have no common baseline, which readers misjudge.

options.label: Stacked areas by default
options.detail: Matches many dashboards; hides each layer's own trend.

items.recommendation: Opt-in stacking for bars and areas: the `.rmd` painter already stacks histogram groups within shared intervals, so stacked bars reuse that path and areas follow the same layer rule; the cost is one field.

items.title: Bar charts
items.question: Keep bar charts as on `main`: grouped slots with one value each, rounding only at the value end, clearance from the zero line and automatic horizontal layout?
items.why: Bars are the default comparison chart; the slot rule decides whether repeated rows are summed silently or rejected.
items.proposed: A `bar` chart draws one bar per category and series slot; `encoding.color` groups bars side by side within each category. Each slot takes exactly one finite value: repeated observations reject that panel with `chart.ambiguous-bar-slot` and "Cannot draw these bars", never a silent sum or pick. A group without a value shows `n/a` at the baseline; a zero draws no length but stays inspectable. Bars start at zero, leave one zero-line stroke of clearance and round only their value end (style `bar-radius`, at most 15% of thickness). Nominal bars with `style.orientation: auto` turn horizontal when names do not fit (FEA-CH-26).

items.title: Bars coloured by their own category
items.question: Keep one full-width bar per category in its own colour when `encoding.color` names the same field as `encoding.x`?
items.why: Colouring each bar by its category is a common single-series request. FEA-CH-06 describes only grouped slots, under which every category would reserve a slot for every colour value and show `n/a` for pairs that cannot occur.
items.proposed: When `encoding.color` names the same field as `encoding.x`, each category draws one full-width bar in its own palette colour; impossible combinations reserve no slots and draw no `n/a`. Hiding a category keeps the other categories' colours. Distinct x and colour fields keep grouped slots (FEA-CH-06) even where their values happen to match.

items.title: Scatter plots and bubbles
items.question: Keep scatter plots with translucent fixed-size points and area-true bubbles through `encoding.size`?
items.why: Fixes how relationships and three-variable comparisons look, and what happens to sizes that cannot be drawn.
items.proposed: A `scatter` chart places one point per row at its x and y values: 4 px circles at 72% opacity, so overlaps stay visible, coloured by `encoding.color`. With `encoding.size`, bubble area is proportional to nonnegative values and the largest bubble has a 16 px radius; zero draws no area but stays inspectable; negative, missing or nonnumeric sizes are omitted with a diagnostic. An outlined 16 px reference circle under the plot names the size field and its value. Axes follow FEA-CH-19; point names follow FEA-CH-28. The default ratio is 4:3.

items.title: Pie charts
items.question: Keep pies with full names and shares around the disk, a wrapped key when crowded, and no "Other" grouping?
items.why: Pies are easy to abuse; this fixes the rules that keep them honest and readable.
items.proposed: A `pie` chart sums `encoding.y` per category into slices that start at 12 o'clock and run clockwise in source order (FEA-CH-09). Names and shares sit around the disk when they fit; otherwise a wrapped key appears below and the chart grows taller instead of abbreviating. Categories are never merged into "Other" or truncated. A positive share that rounds to zero reads `<0.1%` and a partial share that rounds to a whole reads `>99.9%`. A negative value is an error (`negative-pie-value`) and its row is skipped; with no positive values the plot says "No positive values to show".

items.title: Heatmaps
items.question: Keep heatmaps coloured by magnitude on the style's OKLCH ramp, with a diverging arm for negatives, printed values and growing rows?
items.why: Fixes how two-way tables of numbers read, including signs, missing cells and duplicate coordinates.
items.proposed: A `heatmap` colours one cell per x/y pair on the style's three-stop ramp, mixed in OKLCH: zero at the low stop, the rounded largest magnitude at the high stop. Negative values take a second arm with the hue turned 150°, so salience follows magnitude and hue shows sign. Cells of at least 40 × 20 px print their value in ink that contrasts with the cell. Rows are at least 1.6 lines tall and the chart grows with them; names wrap to two lines and the grid transposes when that names every column. Missing values show as outlined `n/a` cells outside the colour scale; two values at one coordinate reject the panel.

items.title: Histograms
items.question: Keep histograms with deterministic bins, three measures and disclosed exclusions?
items.why: Fixes how distributions are binned and what a reader can trust about the bars.
items.proposed: A `histogram` bins numeric `encoding.x` into equal-width intervals (Sturges' count by default, at most 256) or authored `count`, `extent` or `edges`, and draws square, touching bars from zero. The measure is `count`, `proportion` or `density`; with density, bar area is probability. Intervals include their lower edge and exclude the upper, except the last. `encoding.color` stacks groups within a bin; facets share edges. Missing, nonnumeric and out-of-extent rows are counted and disclosed; readouts name the interval and its measure; Table and CSV keep every source row.

items.title: Box plots
items.question: Keep box plots with R-7 quartiles, whiskers at observed values within 1.5 IQR and individually drawn outliers?
items.why: Fixes the statistics behind every box and how they are explained to readers.
items.proposed: A `boxplot` summarises numeric `encoding.y` per category and colour group: the box spans the R-7 quartiles Q1 to Q3 with a median rule, whiskers end at the most extreme observed values within 1.5 × IQR, and points beyond are drawn individually as potential outliers. Without `encoding.x`, one box holds all rows. `style.orientation` is `auto`, `vertical` or `horizontal`; `axes.y` always describes values. Readouts separate derived summaries from original outlier rows; excluded rows are counted. A box is never presented as a confidence interval.

items.title: Interval charts
items.question: Keep interval charts that draw only authored bounds and estimates, computing no statistics of their own?
items.why: Uncertainty charts mislead easily; this fixes that RichView draws exactly what the author supplies.
items.proposed: An `interval` chart draws, per category and colour group, the authored range from `encoding.lower` to `encoding.upper` with end caps, plus an estimate marker only when `encoding.y` supplies one. RichView computes no confidence interval, standard error or distribution; the bounds mean what the author says they mean. A lower bound above its upper bound is an error; zero-width ranges are valid; a repeated category/group pair is an error. Authored value limits clip ranges with a disclosure, while readouts, Table and CSV keep the full values.

items.title: Calendar charts share one painter and one look
items.question: Should calendar line and area charts keep their separate time-series painter with its own defaults, or become a calendar scale inside the one chart painter?
items.why: Today two painters draw lines: calendar charts invent a "Value" axis title, fill areas at 13% instead of 18%, and have their own end labels, readouts, Table, zoom and accessible names, so the same YAML looks and behaves differently depending on whether x holds dates.
items.proposed: A line or area whose x values are all ISO dates, date-times or four-digit year strings uses a UTC calendar scale: calendar-exact ticks (FEA-CH-24), one label row (FEA-CH-25), breaks where a gap exceeds 1.5 times the typical spacing, and source text in readouts. Everything else is shared with the other charts: authored-only axis titles, fills, end labels, legend, readouts, Table, actions and motion. Default ratios follow TYP-18: 2:1 on a calendar axis, 16:9 for other lines and areas. Invalid calendar data, such as a repeated timestamp in one series, shows "Cannot draw this time series" with its diagnostics and never falls back to a categorical chart. FEA-CH-74 lists every calendar-only behaviour of `main` and the card that decides it.

items.title: Time-series features only the JSON spec reaches
items.question: Which features that only the internal JSON spec reaches survive the rewrite, and what happens to the one that leaks into `.rmd` charts: Enter rebases any calendar chart?
items.why: They power the /charts/ page (CO₂, CPI, German power prices), but no `.rmd` author can declare them (ARC-19, TYP-21); porting them costs engine scope without author benefit unless they reach the format. One leaks: Enter on a focused `.rmd` calendar chart rebases it to 100, and nothing on the chart turns it back.

items.title: Compact numbers, zero and currency on axes
items.question: When do axis labels compact to k, M or B, and how do zero and currency print?

items.title: Sparse point labels and author highlights
items.question: Which points get name labels by default, and when are leader lines drawn?
items.why: Daniel: scatter labels are "much too dense"; default to sparse extreme or interesting points, add author highlights with priorities, and keep leaders for forced highlights only. `main` ranks up to 64 candidates by isolation and draws a leader for any label placed more than 12 px from its point, so the fixture scatter names all 12 of its points. PR #67 lowers the cap to 16 and drops labels that would need a leader, which still names every point of a chart with 16 or fewer; its 12 px test is measured from the point's centre, so a bubble wider than about 10 px can never be named without a leader.
items.proposed: By default a chart with `encoding.label` names at most five points, and three when the plot is narrower than 480 px: first the points with the smallest and largest x and y, then the most isolated. Each name sits beside its mark, measured from the mark's edge so large bubbles qualify, without a leader; a name that would collide is hidden and reported as dropped (`density` or `collision`). Points the author highlights (T-CHART-HIGHLIGHTS, TYP-78) are named first, in priority order, on top of the default set, and only they may use a leader when no adjacent position is free. No label overlaps another label, a mark or an axis. Automatic primary values are on for ordinary bars, large stacked-bar parts, lines, unstacked areas and density curves, using the exact corresponding readout text at the author’s precision. Continuous values share a total budget of five, or three when the plot is narrower than 480 px. items.proposed:
Hover draws a crisp ring around the hovered mark: a 1.5 px edge in the paper colour, then one 1.25 px ring in the mark's own colour, with at most a faint tail behind it and no blurred glow. Other bars and packed bubbles keep full strength. In a stacked bar chart the hovered segment takes the ring, its series keeps full strength in every stack and the other series recede to 20%, as they do from the legend (FEA-CH-33). A stacked area and a streamgraph do the same for the layer under the pointer, and the hover dot, with the ring, sits on that layer's upper edge; over no layer, and from the keyboard of a stacked area, every layer keeps full strength and takes a dot with the ring on its edge. Line hover draws the actual filled dot, whole at an axis, with the ring, and every other line-based chart answers the pointer, the keyboard and the legend as a line does: area, band, density, ECDF and streamgraph draw the same dot and ring on each series' own mark (an area's line, a band's centre line, a density curve, an ECDF step) and recede no series on hover; a fill keeps its own strength and follows its series when the legend picks it out. Scatter grows 60% for small points and 25% when sized by a field, with the ring. The flow node strengthens its existing border and takes the ring in that border's colour. Alluvial and Sankey nodes and ribbons take the dark outline of the marks that thin gaps set apart and the rest of the chart stays as it is, as before 12 November (Daniel, 25 November: “alluvia and sankey please also with black boarder highlights intsead of dimmings rest of stuff”), and OHLC keeps its band in the mark's own colour. Every other filled mark answers the pointer with a dark outline, and nothing else on the chart changes. A mark with room around it takes a 1.5 px ink line at 85% over a 3.5 px paper line, inside one flat 4 px band of its own colour at 25% that starts 1.75 px out: funnel stages, bullet bars, candlesticks, dumbbell dots, waterfall bars, box plots, intervals, pareto, combo and Gantt bars, lollipop and dot-plot dots, tree and network nodes. A line inside the mark's own box, such as a box plot's median, takes nothing, and a whisker or wick comes back in its own colour between the lines. items.title: Charts in print and PDF
items.question: Keep `main`'s print rules for charts?
items.why: PDF export (F-EXPORT-PDF) needs complete, settled, legible charts.
items.proposed:
In print and PDF, charts show their settled view (the current view in browser print, the authored initial view in PDF export) without actions, overview strip, readout or zoom brush; legend entries print as plain text; a chart is at most 60% of the page height and never splits across pages; dark styles print with their light counterpart. An expanded chart prints in place, not as a modal. Where a chart does not fit the space left on a page, it floats to the top of the next page and the text after it flows up to fill the gap (FEA-RP-43). In PDF export every chart is vector output from the engine's vector renderer (Daniel's INT-31 answer, FEA-RP-43).

Open question for Daniel: what browser Print (FEA-RP-34) shows for a WebGL chart, since only PDF export converts charts to vector. Options: the canvas as drawn on screen, a raster at screen resolution that needs its drawing buffer kept or a redraw before printing; the runtime redrawing each chart at print resolution on `beforeprint`, still raster; or vector charts drawn by the runtime for print, which needs the vector renderer in the report runtime (PRF-31) and goes beyond “only PDF export”.

items.title: Map, flow and pivot-table checks
items.question: What proves the map, flow and pivot-table elements your FEA-CH-01 answer adds, which no feature card specifies yet?
items.why: They cannot be tested before they are specified, and pivot aggregation is a new way to show a wrong number.
items.proposed:
Each element first gets feature and type cards (parts 04a, 04b and 05); these checks come with them.

- **Map:** boundaries and geographic data come from the report folder or ship with RichView, never from a server at read time (ARC-11); projected positions match known coordinates; values equal the source at the author's precision; labels do not collide; zoom and pan pass model tests; the offline file works.
- **Flow:** the same source gives the same layout, natively and in Wasm; labels never clip; edges do not cross nodes; a one-node edit moves few other nodes, measured; it reads as an ordered list to assistive technology. Nova flow is the reference to improve on.
- **Pivot table:** every aggregation equals a reference computation on fixtures with nulls, decimals and dates (DEL-16); totals and subtotals add up; sorting and expand or collapse work by keyboard; print shows every row; its CSV equals what is displayed.

options.label: Specs first, then these checks
options.detail: Nothing is built untested; the elements wait for their cards.

options.label: Build now, test like charts
options.detail: Faster start; map projection, flow layout and aggregation have no dedicated oracle.

items.recommendation: Specs first, then these checks.

items.title: Chart accessibility checks with WebGL
items.question: Once FEA-CH-55 decides how screen-reader users reach a canvas chart, what proves it?
items.why: FEA-RP-49 makes WCAG 2.2 AA a gate, and an automated audit sees a canvas only as its container's name.
items.proposed: Whatever layer FEA-CH-55 chooses (an ARIA mark layer, the Table, or both), the gate checks it against the geometry model: every figure has a name and summary in its HTML, also when the chart shows ARC-05's notice; the summary's facts match the data, per type, at the author's precision; a mark layer lists every mark with the readout's text; keyboard inspection reaches every mark in order (FEA-CH-56); the Table shows the source rows at the author's precision (FEA-CH-37). Nothing a reader or assistive technology can reach, including ARIA labels, live regions and attributes in the DOM, carries more digits than the author chose for that element (FEA-CH-37). The server pages for approval, the source editor and the owner menu join DEL-58's audit. The VoiceOver pass stays a standing gap until it can be driven reliably (DEL-58).

options.label: Model-checked accessibility layer
options.detail: What assistive technology gets is proven against the same model readers see.

options.label: Automated audit only
options.detail: As DEL-58; passes a canvas with a name and nothing else.

items.recommendation: Model-checked accessibility layer.
